items.title: A hidden ocean change near Antarctica could have global consequences
items.excerpt: The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say. In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years. The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen , a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India. items.title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
items.excerpt: Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters. Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation. One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission , an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026. Read full article Comments

items.title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
items.excerpt: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country's occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely—or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions. In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread. South Carolina's measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania's ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it. Read full article Comments

items.title: China's top-secret spaceplane can't hide in low-Earth orbit
items.excerpt: A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military's X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image. The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force. The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space. Read full article Comments

items.title: macro-inc / macro
items.excerpt: Sign up · Docs · Book demo · Website · Feature requests · Contribute · Hiring Macro is the all-in-one workspace for you and your team. It unifies email + messages + docs + tasks + agents + CRM into a single fast interface with shared team-level memory. Everything in your workspace is @linked and searchable so your team (and your agents) never have to switch tools. # Why Macro We built Macro because we wanted a single operating system for our startup. There are many good software products, and we used them all — Slack, Linear, Notion, HubSpot, and Superhuman — but they don't work together as one system. As we scaled our last venture to ~20 people things started to break: every team got their own tools and the company was held together by MCP and Zapier. The company was not computable. It was chaotic. Macro is a complete redesign of work software from the ground up as a single system. Designed by us in NYC and Toronto, dogfooded by our team of ~15 for two years. Built in SolidJS and Rust for speed and reliability. We're focused on building something that any small company or team at a larger company can use as their "operating system". # Features Macro is composed of 'blocks' designed to be modular, extensible, and work together like Lego. For each block, we studied the best prior art and tried to make it even better. Each surface is purpose-built for its job rather than composed from a generic block primitive — but every one of them shares the same backend; cross-references…

items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. items.title: Prompt Injection Is Just the Start of AI Agent Security (Here's What You Need)
items.excerpt: Learn more about agent security here: https://fandf.co/4i1Qs4u My second brain helps me run my entire business, and that means giving it access to a lot of my systems and data, so I check everything it pulls in and keep its access limited. That works for one agent. A company has agents running across cloud platforms and employee devices, and IT has to know which ones exist, who owns them, and what they can reach. Microsoft is expanding Project Perception, building on Agent 365, to secure AI agents at scale. It gives agents their own identity, scopes their access to the task, and contains them as risk changes, without taking away employees' approved access. Dynamic Permissions gives agents task-specific, time-bound access to supported resources, and separately, risk-based access controls evaluate supported agent actions using current risk and policy. Your team reviews and approves protections before they're enforced. Thanks to Microsoft for working with me on this!

items.title: This video was edited by Opus in a single prompt
items.excerpt: i edited this video in 1 prompt... this is getting scary... i filmed this video 16 minutes ago... Edited 100% with Opus 5.5. I uploaded a single video of myself (with many mistakes). Opus went on to: 1. Analyze the transcript 2. Search Twitter for the relevant B-roll (Claude Code literally calls GrokBot for this step) 3. Scrape the Twitter video assets 4. Cut the video based on mistakes and word gaps 5. Build out the Blender scene from a template 6. Build the UI and components of each shot (my Blender scene has 4 shots: a computer, phone, table, and board) 7. It took screenshots of every section, analyzed and fixed them 8. Synced every shot, zoom, and animation to the exact words I say 9. Animated a robot arm placing real logos on the table right when I mention them 10. Drew the whiteboard ending with logos and graphics instead of text 11. Pulled a cutaway from the creator's own video, with his voice 12. Rendered all 3,487 frames on RunPod cloud GPUs in under 20 minutes, for less than $1 13. Put me in the bottom third only when I'm talking, so the B-roll stays full screen 14. Added word-by-word captions, sound effects, and music 15. Uploaded it to my Google Drive, ready to post Will be making a full youtube video this week explaining it. I want to learn a little more about how cloud rendering works before making video, as well as figuring out what the best provider is. items.title: The Worst 48 Hours in Internet History

items.title: Smaller NLAs and probes read eval awareness as well as full size NLAs
items.excerpt: TLDR: We distill and train various Natural Language Autoencoders (“NLAs”) to read Qwen3.6-27b’s internal states. A 2B NLA distilled from a 27B NLA matches it on reading agentic misalignment and eval awareness, but is much worse on obscure facts. An NLA trained with extra alignment-focused RL didn’t improve on anything. A linear probe trained on 2B-generated labels matches a 27B NLA + LLM judge on reading eval awareness, at a tiny fraction of the cost. Eval awareness results come from 76 technical tasks with injected cues. We haven’t yet tested how far they generalise. Introduction NLAs train a pair of LLMs: one to construct text from the information in a given LLM’s vector, and the other to reconstruct the vector. The constructed text is an imperfect but useful indicator of what the model is thinking about at any token position. These are expensive to run, as they involve generating whole paragraphs of tokens to read one token of thought. We distill a trained NLA reader for Qwen3.6-27b to a Qwen3.5-2b model, and train the model after distillation to boost its performance. The reason: to read Qwen3.6-27b’s (“Qwen”) activations at a much lower cost, which if performant could enable reading LLMs’ workspaces at a larger scale. Smaller NLAs could also generate data to train better probes for eval awareness, intent to deceive, suspicion of monitoring, and other things which would be useful to see in many circumstances. items.title: Self-Experiment Results on Caffeine, Exercise and Meditation
items.excerpt: Last year, I posted the results of a self-experiment on Melatonin . This year, I ran another self-experiment from January to June, the results of which I'll lay out in this post. Tl;dr : I randomized three interventions on a daily basis and tracked several metrics throughout the day to see what the short-term effects are. Interventions centered on coffee intake, meditation, and doing jumping jacks, all of which happened primarily in the morning. Caveats apply (n = 1, nothing was blinded, some analyses slightly differ from my "preregistration"). items.title: Why Global Trepanation?
items.excerpt: A friend asked me to investigate the following mystery: why do 5-10% of skulls from 10,000 BC to 3,000 BC, all over the world, have holes in them? Why do bone growth patterns indicate that most skull-hole-havers survived years after their holes were drilled, even though brain surgery today requires careful sterilization (and frequently, prophylactic antibiotics) to prevent fatal infections? And why did everyone stop doing this sometime around the beginning of recorded history? Was it cultural diffusion? No. Trepanation (the technical term for drilling a hole in the skull) was common across Europe and South America, with scattered cases in Africa and other continents. The Old and New Worlds had limited contact after about 10,000 BC, and most customs don’t survive for five thousand plus years with no reason. Was it good medicine? Sort of, but not in a way that entirely solves the mystery. Trepanation is an effective treatment for epidural hematoma: a patient ruptures a blood vessel in their skull, filling the cranial cavity with blood, and the pressure rises so high that it squashes various vital blood vessels and brain regions, killing the patient. Drilling a hole in the skull releases the blood, relieves the pressure, and saves the patient’s life. This is great, but these kinds of hematomas are very rare today: about 1/100,000 per year. So how do you get 5-10% of people trepanned? I think there are two reasons. First, prehistory was very violent . People were frequently…

items.title: Against Against Handover
items.excerpt: The latest bugbear is “AI successionism”, the belief that AIs should succeed humans as rulers of Earth. But some critiques fail to distinguish between two different ideas. True successionism says that AIs should take over, killing humans or steamrolling over their interests. This is very bad: a compact description of the thing that AI safety is against. Handoverism says that humans should prioritize their own interests, but that those interests may be well-served by having aligned AIs in positions of control. Some people in AI safety, including me, find this latter position plausible. We are being lumped in with the true successionists as fellow travelers in an anti-human direction ( 1 , 2 , 3 , although thanks for commenters pointing out that these essays do at least make the distinction). It may seem counterintuitive that human interests can be served by having AIs in positions of control. But I think the counterintuitiveness comes from a nationalist outlook where ‘the State is the highest expression of the life of a people’, and the role of leadership is for someone of your own ethnic group to be the leader so you can feel good about being on top. The liberal outlook is that the state exists to help individuals fulfill their goals. At the risk of desacralizing the state a little more than I mean to, it’s a service provider, dispensing coordination, public order, redistribution, and other good things. Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. items.title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. I contrast a stopwatch view, on which time saved is whatever the clock records, with a ledger view, on which it is a counterfactual that has to be read next to the errors the work lets through, and I argue for the latter. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. I give a baseline model of checking in which, until the model is good enough not to check, a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on how good the model is; checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate; and over-trust buys minutes on the clock at a larger cost in total minutes. I show what randomized studies can and cannot identify, and I replicate METR's developer study from its public data: the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depending on the estimand (34% without adjusting for a chance imbalance), and AI helped on somewhere between 3% and 82% of them. Finally, I restate the published record, with stated bounds in place of imported point assumptions. In GDPval's own review-every-output workflow, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x; the consultants outside the frontier were faster, and more often wrong. Last, I test two of the model's predictions in a small pre-specified experiment on AI reviewers checking AI…

items.title: Enhancing Deep Learning Model Performance through Data Generation Strategies: Classification of Olive Tree Diseases
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models are highly effective in a wide range of domains, particu larly in plant disease diagnosis. However, their performance is often limited by challenges such as insufficient data and class imbalance. In our work, we propose a comprehensive data generation strategy to overcome these limitations. First, we apply various data generation techniques, including traditional augmentation methods, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic image generation using Deep Convolu tional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs), to create new data samples. Second, we exploit this generated data in three scenarios: (S1) balancing class distribution in the original dataset, (S2) increasing the number of samples per class, and (S3) expanding the dataset while maintaining balanced classes. Third, we evaluate the impact of these data distributions (S1, S2, S3) on model perfor mance using the EfficientNetV2B0 architecture with pre-trained and fine-tuned weights. The experimental results show a substantial improvement in classifica tion accuracy, emphasizing the critical role of data diversity and class balance. These findings highlight the effectiveness and adaptability of the proposed strat egy of data generation and distribution for enhancing dataset quality, offering promising applications in plant disease detection and precision agriculture.

items.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information…

items.title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.

items.title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new…

items.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
items.excerpt: Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: Minimize coordination Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. items.title: The next developer interface is ambient intelligence
items.excerpt: For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine. AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls. We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different. AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. items.excerpt: In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26), 23% of new light-duty vehicles sold in the United States were hybrid electric, battery electric, or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, down slightly from 24% in 3Q25. Between 3Q25 and 3Q26, hybrid electric vehicles continued to gain market share, reaching 16% of light-duty vehicle sales. items.title: U.S. small-scale solar generation has quadrupled in the last decade
items.excerpt: We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country-California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida-are in regions with more abundant solar resources. Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives.

items.title: How food companies turn taxpayer-funded school meals into a market for ultra-processed foods
items.excerpt: Key findings Ultra-processed food companies heavily market their products and brands through a program that lets schools send fresh USDA-supplied ingredients for processing. Most become convenience foods, including ultra-processed foods, which have been linked to diabetes, obesity, cancer, and other health harms. Researchers say school food is designed to benefit food companies, not children’s health. Schools need investment to build capacity to serve fresh, minimally processed meals, they say. Tyson Foods markets its “pop-them-in-your-mouth” popcorn chicken bites to school cafeterias, promising they can go from freezer to serving line in minutes. The company also offers school districts a calculator to estimate how much government-supplied chicken and other ingredients to send for processing. Tyson isn’t alone. It’s part of a much larger system in which public school districts send taxpayer-funded ingredients to private manufacturers, whose products and marketing shape what children eat. School lunches that start with government-supplied chicken, mozzarella cheese, flour or tomato paste often take this detour and become packaged, mostly ultra-processed foods (UPFs) by the time they reach children’s plates. “I’m sending my beef [from USDA commodities] to somebody like Don Lee and getting hamburgers. items.title: Babies exposed to microplastics and hormone-disrupting chemicals through formula, plastic bottles, infant feeding supplies
items.excerpt: Key findings One study estimated that polypropylene baby bottles can release up to 16.2 million microplastic particles per liter of formula during conventional formula preparation. Studies detected microplastics and chemicals, including phthalates and bisphenols, in formula, packaging, and other feeding products. Some studies reported changes in gut bacteria, immune-related markers, and hormone function, but the review could not establish whether exposure causes harm. Babies may consume millions of microplastics and traces of harmful chemicals through infant formula, plastic bottles, and other feeding products, according to a scientific review. The review, published in September in Environmental Science and Pollution Research , examined 27 studies of these products published over the past decade. They show evidence of tiny plastic particles and endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) , including phthalates , bisphenols , per-fluoroalkyl substances ( PFAS , or “forever chemicals”), and organophosphorus flame retardants (OPEs) and their byproducts. Overall, the findings highlight an emerging problem with “profound” implications for public health, the authors say. “This review highlights the daily, unnoticed, and poorly regulated exposure to various chemical agents that occurs today,” they wrote. “The discovery of plastic particles in infant formula and baby bottles, even before their first use, raises ethical questions about the safety of products intended for this population.”…

items.title: FBI Files: Civil Rights Era
items.excerpt: Background Movements for civil rights were a worldwide series of political movements for equality before the law that peaked in the 1960s. In many situations it took the form of campaigns of civil resistance aimed at achieving change through nonviolent forms of resistance. In some situations it was accompanied, or followed, by civil unrest and armed rebellion. The process was long and tenuous in many countries, and many of these movements did not fully achieve their goals, although the efforts of these movements did lead to improvements in the legal rights of previously oppressed groups of people. Below are files of prominent people and events.
